newsitem.title: USA: Savio, leader of Free Speech Movement, dies.
newsitem.headline: Savio, leader of Free Speech Movement, dies.

text.p: Mario Savio, a leader of the Free Speech Movement which jolted the University of California during the 1960s, died in a California hospital Wednesday, a hospital spokeswoman said. He was 53.
Savio had been in a coma since being admitted last Saturday to Columbia Palm Drive Hospital in Sebastopol, 50 miles north of San Francisco, chief nursing officer Sharon Enos said.
Savio's wife, brother and son were among family members at his bedside when he died on Wednesday afternoon, Enos said, adding: "It was a peaceful death."
Enos would not disclose the cause of death, but news reports said Savio suffered a heart attack over the weekend.
Savio, married with three children, lived in Sebastopol and was a lecturer at Sonoma State University where he taught math and philosophy.

Savio became well-known in 1964 when he urged fellow students at the University of California at Berkeley to shut down the campus to protest a ban on political activity on campus. The ban came at a time when student activists were trying to recruit others into the civil rights movement.
The Free Speech Movement sparked years of upheavals on U.S. university campuses, later to be torn by Vietnam War protests.
Savio's most famous moment came in 1964 when police arrested activist Jack Weinberg for handing out leaflets on the Berkeley campus and put him in a police car.
Scores of students sat down around the police car, refusing to move for 32 hours. Savio was one of the students who climbed onto the roof of the car and delivered a speech that electrified the crowd.
After weeks of marches, sit-ins and a strike, the university gave way and lifted the ban on political activity.
In recent years, Savio had spoken out publicly on a variety of social issues, opposing an initiative passed by California voters this week to dismantle many state affirmative action programmes.
Savio and other former Free Speech Movement leaders returned to Berkeley in 1994 for an event marking the 30th anniversary of the movement.
